title: Read All About It
briefing: A news site has 2 million articles. Traffic climbs from 6,000 to 20,000 requests per second over the first minute, and about two minutes in, breaking news pushes it to 26,000 for half a minute.

Every request needs 0.5ms of CPU on an app server, then one trip to the data: 95% read an article, the rest post a comment, which writes to the database. Even the biggest database can't serve every read on its own.

Readers are predictable: a few hundred stories get most of the traffic, and most of the archive is barely touched. A cache keeps popular articles in memory, so reads that find them there never reach the database. Each article takes about 100 KB, and the cache starts empty.
debrief: The database is the bottleneck. At the 26,000 req/s peak there are 24,700 reads and 1,300 writes every second. A large database does 10,000 reads or 4,000 writes a second, so the writes alone keep it a third busy, and the reads would need two and a half more databases.

Article popularity follows Zipf's law: the 10th most popular story gets a tenth of the traffic of the top one, the 100th a hundredth. So a cache that holds a small slice of the archive catches most of the reads. An 8 GB cache holds 80,000 articles, 4% of them, and those 4% get about 79% of the reads. A 2 GB cache holds 20,000, which get 69%.

The hit rate decides the database's load. At the peak, a 77% hit rate leaves about 5,700 reads a second for the database: with the writes it's around 90% busy and keeps up. At 69%, 7,700 reads plus the writes need 110% of it, and requests start timing out.

Two things keep a cache below its best. It starts cold: it only learns what's popular as articles are read, which is why the slow morning ramp matters. And values expire: an article stays cached for its TTL, so a rarely read one has usually expired by its next read. With a 10-second TTL the same 8 GB cache hits only about 65%.
Before sizing a cache, ask how skewed the reads are. In front of skewed traffic, a cache is the cheapest way to multiply a database's read capacity. The next level shows when it isn't.

solutions.name: A medium cache in front of a large database
solutions.explanation: An 8 GB cache holds the 80,000 most-read articles and serves about 76% of reads, a little more at the peak. The large database takes the misses and every write, about 90% busy at the height of the spike.

antiSolutions.name: Large database, no cache
antiSolutions.explanation: 19,000 reads a second against a database that does 10,000. It falls behind as soon as traffic passes about 9,000 requests per second.

antiSolutions.name: Biggest database, no cache
antiSolutions.explanation: An xlarge database does 20,000 reads a second, but the writes take an eighth of it, so it's overloaded from 20,000 req/s. It's also over budget.

antiSolutions.name: A small cache
antiSolutions.explanation: A 2 GB cache holds 20,000 articles and hits 69%. Enough at 20,000 req/s, but the breaking-news spike pushes the database past 100%.

antiSolutions.name: Values that expire too soon
antiSolutions.explanation: The right size, but with a 10-second TTL: less popular articles expire before anyone reads them again, the hit rate falls to 65%, and the spike overloads the database.
